1. What Is a Temple? A temple is a consecrated place associated with the presence and worship of a deity. In Hindu traditions, it is
often understood not simply as a building that houses an image, but as a carefully ordered sacred
environment. Its design, orientation, proportions, images and ritual sequence can express ideas about the
universe and the relationship between human life and the divine. The innermost shrine, usually called the garbhagriha or sanctum, contains the principal deity. Worshippers
approach it through one or more halls, gateways or courtyards.

3. The Temple as a Sacred Plan
Traditional temple design is guided by systems of proportion, orientation and spatial organisation. Texts on
architecture and sculpture, often grouped under the broad term Vastu Shastra and related Shilpa Shastra
traditions, discuss the planning of sacred buildings. Practices differ across regions and historical periods, so no
single manual describes every temple. A common plan centres on the garbhagriha, the sanctum where the principal deity is installed. It is often
relatively small and intentionally restrained. The mandapa, or pillared hall, provides space for worshippers and
ritual activities. Larger temples may contain several halls, each with a distinct function.

12. Festivals, Pilgrimage and Sacred Geography
Temple festivals transform sacred spaces and surrounding streets. Annual celebrations may mark a deity's
mythology, seasonal cycles, agricultural rhythms or local history. Processions can carry festival images through
designated routes, allowing the deity to visit the community beyond the sanctum. Chariot festivals, known in many regions as rath yatras or by local names, are especially visible events. Decorated processional vehicles are pulled by devotees, accompanied by music, offerings and crowds. Other
festivals feature lamps, flower decorations, water rituals, dance, theatre and communal meals. Pilgrimage connects temples into networks of sacred geography. Some journeys focus on a single shrine;
others form circuits across mountains, rivers, coastlines or regions. The journey itself may be understood as an
act of devotion, discipline and renewal. Sacred geography is shaped by stories and memory. A temple may be linked to a river's source, a hill, a forest,
a legendary event or the life of a saint.

TEMPLES  |  AN INTRODUCTION TO INDIAN TEMPLE HERITAGE
12
11. Daily Worship and Ritual Life
Daily temple worship varies according to deity, region, lineage and local custom. A typical sequence may
include the opening of the shrine, preparation of the deity, offerings, recitation, lamp ceremonies and the
distribution of prasada. The schedule may be organised into several services across the day. Puja is a broad term for worship involving offerings and devotional acts. These may include flowers, water,
food, incense, lamps, music and sacred recitation. In some traditions, the deity is treated with the hospitality
shown to an honoured guest: awakened, bathed, dressed, fed and offered rest. Darshan refers to the act of seeing and being seen by the deity. For many devotees, this encounter is central to
temple worship. The arrangement of the sanctum, lamps and queue may shape how darshan takes place. Pradakshina, or circumambulation, involves moving clockwise around a sacred object or shrine. It expresses
reverence and places the devotee's movement in relation to the sacred centre.
